# The Kitchen at 2 A.M.

The tile is always cold. That's the first thing, the thing you feel before you're fully awake, before the brain catches up to the body's decision to walk. You step barefoot out of the bedroom and the world announces itself in a small shock of cold against the soles, and for a half-second you are just an animal navigating by temperature and gravity, not a person with a name and a Tuesday morning that's waiting for you somewhere beyond the walls.

The kitchen is the one room in the house that doesn't care what time it is. It's a room built for the middle of the night as much as for the noon rush. Someone, in the original construction of this house, decided the kitchen would sit in the corner, the far corner, the one you'd have to cross the whole living room to reach. And now here I am, four years after the house was built, crossing the living room at 2:14 a.m. because the water in my glass on the nightstand has gone flat and the memory of it is somehow more unbearable than the thirst itself.

The fridge hums. I always forget how loud it is until it's the only sound. A low, steady, mechanical breathing, as if the machine is the only living thing in the room and I'm the ghost. The light above the stove is too bright, a hospital-white glow that makes the countertop look like an operating table. I turn it off and the overhead fixture, the one that used to work, would be a dimmer alternative, but the bulb burned out three months ago and I keep meaning to replace it and I never do. So I stand in a dark kitchen and navigate by the blue-white glow of the fridge door and the pale rectangle of moonlight through the window.

I fill the glass. The tap sputters first, that little burst of sediment-tasting water that tells you the pipes have been sitting still for hours, that the whole building has been asleep and the water has been sitting in them like a slow thought. I wait it out. The water clears. I drink.

And then I just stand there.

This is the thing about 2 a.m. that no one warns you about. It's not that you can't sleep. You can. Your body is capable of it. But something in the architecture of the night, the specific quality of the dark outside the window, the silence that isn't silence but a low static, the way the house has stopped being a performance and become just a structure with a heartbeat you can feel in the pipes—something in all of it makes the mind go quiet in a way that is almost violent. The constant, low-grade narration you run all day, the commentary, the to-do lists, the replays of conversations, the small anxieties about whether you sounded weird in that email, the planning, the *narrating*—it just stops. And in the silence where it was, you are confronted with the fact that you are a person who is alone in a room, and that this is normal, and that it is also, in a way that's hard to articulate, profoundly strange.

I lean against the counter. The wood is smooth, worn to a pale gold where years of elbows have rested. I think about the people who stood here before me, in the years before the house was built, when this was someone else's kitchen, or not a kitchen at all, when this was a field or a road or nothing. I think about how the house was built by hands, hundreds of hands, a man who set the joists, a woman who ran the plumbing, a kid who was paid fifteen dollars an hour to haul drywall and whose face I will never know. And I think: I am the latest person in a long line of people who have stood in this exact spot, breathing the air of this room, maybe thinking about something, maybe thinking about nothing. The wood remembers the pressure of their elbows. The tile remembers the cold feet. The fridge hums for all of them, past and future, a mechanical rosary.

I turn on the stove light. I look at the burner, the four small rings of iron, the little dials that I have used a hundred times in the same way, the same half-turn, the same click. I turn them back off. I look at the window. The moon is almost full, a pale disc behind a thin smear of cloud. There's a tree outside, the big maple that the previous owners planted, and its branches are bare now, November, and the moonlight catches them in a way that makes them look like veins, like the circulatory system of the dark.

I think about sleep. Not the lack of it, but the sleep itself, the thing I'm going to go back to. The strange experience of your body saying *I am going to stop being a person for eight hours.* The slow dissolve. The way dreams are just the brain tidying up, folding the day into the closet, putting the small important things on a hook by the door so you can grab them in the morning. And the way, if you wake at 2 a.m., the closet is open, the clothes are out, and you have to stand there and decide whether to go back in or walk around the house barefoot, feeling the cold, drinking water that tastes like the pipes.

I drink the rest of the glass. I put it back in the cabinet, the one above the sink, where the glasses live in a row, catching the moonlight in their rims, little circles of pale light, like eyes. I pull the chain for the bathroom light on the way back. The living room is dark and warm, the thermostat doing its quiet work, the couch holding the shape of my body from the afternoon. I can hear the house settling, the small ticks and pops of wood contracting in the cold.

I get back into bed. The sheets are warm where I was, and cold where I wasn't, and for a moment it's both at once, and I think that might be the whole thing, the whole life, the warm and the cold in the same sheet, the same breath. The fridge hums in the next room. The moon is behind the cloud. The maple's bare branches press against the glass like something trying to get in, or just resting, just leaning, the way a person leans against a window and looks out and thinks about nothing and thinks about everything and then, finally, closes their eyes.

The tile will be cold in the morning. The water will be cold. The light will be too bright.

I close my eyes.
